desc:
Given a non-negative integer n, count how many times the digit 1 appears in the decimal representations of all integers from 0 to n inclusive. A number such as 111 contributes three.

n = 13  -> 6   (1, 10, 11 (two), 12, 13)
n = 0   -> 0
n = 99  -> 20

Looping over every number is too slow when n is close to a billion.
hints: Count the ones separately for each digit position (units, tens, hundreds, ...) and add the totals.
For position with place value m, split n into high = n // (m*10), cur = (n // m) % 10 and low = n % m. Full cycles of the lower positions contribute high * m ones.
Then add depending on cur: if cur > 1 an extra full block of m ones; if cur == 1 the partial block adds low + 1; if cur == 0 nothing more.
editorial: Look at one position at a time, say the hundreds place with m = 100. As the numbers run from 0 upward, that digit is 1 for exactly 100 consecutive numbers (x100 to x199) in every window of 1000 consecutive numbers. So the high full windows (high = n // 1000) contribute high * 100 ones.

Then consider the incomplete last window, which starts with the hundreds digit equal to cur. If cur = 0 the digit has not reached 1 yet: no extra. If cur = 1, the digit is 1 for the numbers from the start of the hundreds-1 block up to n, which is low + 1 numbers, where low = n % 100. If cur ≥ 2 the whole hundreds-1 block is complete and adds 100.
Repeat for every place value up to the highest digit of n. The loop runs at most 10 times. The total fits in 32 bits for n ≤ 109 (the maximum is 900,000,001).
